newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Expert pins ZCCM woes on S.Africa mkt, Zambia govt.
newsitem.headline: Expert pins ZCCM woes on S.Africa mkt, Zambia govt.

text.p: A mining expert on Friday blamed Zambia Consolidated Copper Mines Ltd's (ZCCM) declining performance on ill-conceived contracts with South African suppliers and government interference in the company's operations.

Central Bank director and former ZCCM senior executive Mbita Kabalika said the opening of the South African market had increased the company's supply and transportation costs, pushing its performance down.

"The opening of the South African market, instead of contributing to cost controls and quick delivery of spares, has had a negative impact on cost," Kabalika told an international economic conference organised by the Bank.

"Instead of taking a hard, strategic and dispassionate look at the South African market in relation to its purchasing and supply considerations, ZCCM plunged headlong into this market almost blindly," Kabalika added.
The former ZCCM executive said South African dealers had hiked commodity and transport costs in response to ZCCM demand.
"If strategic sourcing and transportation had been actively pursued, they would have substantially contributed to cost control and eventually to profitability," he added.
Government tolerance of mismanagement and of political interference had also contributed to the company's poor performance.

"Compounded by these developments has been government's deliberate failure to police and control the conglomerate. No one in government, it appears, seems to have had the willingness or the stomach to rein in the maladies," he said.

The company had failed to take advantage of an improved business environment to improve its performance, which continued to fall even after the export retention scheme was expanded to allow it to retain 100 percent of its proceeds, and mineral export taxes were abolished.
Meanwhile, the central bank started had paying ZCCM at the prevailing rate for its foreign currency and corporate tax was reduced from 40 percent to 35 percent in April 1993.
"However, these favourable developments were never seized upon and have to date done little to engender the expected boost in the production of metals," Kabalika said.
He said ZCCM production had continued to fall over the past decade, from a peak of 472,084 tonnes in 1988 to 313,923 tonnes in 1996 -- a 33 percent drop.
"The ZCCM problem has become so unmanageable that the best resolution appears to be its quick privatisation," Kabalika said.
ZCCM -- the country's largest earner of foreign exchange -- is currently in the process of privatising its assets, including copper and cobalt mines.
